content.title: Comment
content.comment: Dear reviewers, thank you very much for your time and comments. As stated in our paper, our results are a joint effort of three training methodology improvements: a semantic aware reconstruction target, a more effective decoder design, and a more efficient sampling based on patch importance. Previous works like MaskFeat and MVP enhanced one training methodology. Our work also improved the same training methodology but on a different architecture. However, our work contained two other contributions that were not explored by previous works. Our ablation studies show that 62.5%-77.2% of the accuracy gains over previous SOTAs are due to the our contributions not existent in previous works. Our method advances the state-of-the-art on a variety of tasks. We believe that our paper contains insightful findings that can help future researches. We also noticed that we must have communicated with reviewer HXLR in our previous submission. Although we have addressed all the concerns in our previous rebuttal thoroughly, we did not receive concrete feedbacks about our comments. The reviews here are simply copied from previous, disregarding our improvements and updated results in the submission. We decided to withdraw our submission.

content.title: Response.3
content.comment:
Q5. The improvements of ViT large size model are much smaller compared with ViT-Base. The number 86.7 is comparable with data2vec and peco that only utilize imagenet-1k for pretraining. It seems that the model does not scale well with the model size.

A5. The number you listed is outdated. We have conducted new experiemnts on ViT-Large and reported new number in our submission.
Our improvements on ViT-Large is consistent with those on ViT-Base. From Table 1, MILAN achieved 87.8% top-1 at 224x224 resolution and 88.3\% top-1 at 384x384 resolution on ImageNet. When using ViT-Large, MILAN outperforms data2vec and PeCo by 1.2\% and 1.3\%, respectively. The results clearly show that MILAN scales well with model sizes.

Q6. Because the method is based on MaskFeat and MVP, the result difference seems to come from MaskFeat with CLIP (i.e., MVP), instead of the components proposed in the paper. The analysis part is not insightful enough to show why the method is significantly different from MaskFeat and MVP.

A6. MaskFeat and MVP only replaces the reconstruction targets. However, changing the reconstruction targets alone (MAE+ CLIP or MVP-like method) cannot achieve the optimal performance. As shown in our ablation studies in Table 5 (finetuning on ImageNet) and 6 (semantic segmentation on ADE20K), the majority of the accuracy gains come from the proposed prompting decoder architecture and semantic aware sampling in our method. We also provided visualization analysis of learned representations in Figure 3 (Appendix). Compared with MAE+CLIP, MILAN can better extract the important visual contents inside the images, indicating that the proposed prompting decoder and semantic aware sampling contribute significantly to learning higher quality visual representations.

content.title: Response.2
content.comment:
Q2. Many experiments were conducted with 400 epochs. It's unfair to directly compare the results with previous work, in which most results used 300 epochs. The experiments can be improved to make the comparisons more fair.

A2. In Table 1 results on ImageNet, most of our compared methods pretrained for 800 epochs (e.g., BEiT, mc-BEiT, PeCo, SimMIM, data2vec) and 1600 epochs (e.g., MaskFeat, CAE, MAE, iBOT). Our MILAN method pretrained for 400 epochs only, while achieving the best accuracy.

Q3. The work heavily relies on the pretrained CLIP models. It's somewhat unfair to directly compare with previous models. The work FD-CLIP (Contrastive Learning Rivals Masked Image Modeling in Fine-tuning via Feature Distillation) shows that knowledge distillaiton can get comparable results as the submission. It's questionable that whether the proposed methods (masking selection and decoder arch) were helpful or not. Moreover, the ablation studies are only conducted on CLIP targets. The ablation results based on SLIP and other downstream tasks can be added.

A3. In Table 1 and 2, we compared with method that also heavily uses CLIPs models, e.g., MVP. In finetuning task on ImageNet, MILAN outperforms MVP by 1.0\% and 1.5\% top-1 accuracy for ViT-Base and Large. In linear probing task, MILAN outperforms MVP by 4.5\%. FD-CLIP is a concurrent work that proposed feature distillation method. Using ViT-Base, MILAN outperforms FD-CLIP by 0.5\% top-1 accuracy in ImageNet finetuning task.

The effectiveness of our prompting decoder and semantic aware masking are consistently observed in our ablation studies in both ImageNet finetuning task (Table 5) and semantic segmentation task (Table 6). Our extensive ablation studies showed that replacing the reconstruction target alone (like MVP) cannot achieve the optimal performance. Majority of the accuracy gains come from the prompting decoder and the semantic aware sampling.

Q4. Table 5 suggests that the prompt decoder is not helpful to results, i.e., both #3 vs #1, and #5 vs #4 indicate that the prompt decoder has no gain. The motivation of the new decoder arch is not strong enough. More analysis can be added to support the claims. Longer training epochs also does not significantly improve the performance as shown in Table 5.

A4. In Table 5 ablation study, we showed that MILAN without prompting decoder degraded by 1.3\% top-1 accuracy compared to MILAN with prompting decoder. This clearly indicated that effectiveness of prompting decoder. The ablation study also corroborated our claim that the model architecture and training methodology are tightly coupled with the reconstruction target and they need to be adapted accordingly. 

In MAE, the model reconstructs raw pixels containing low-level image statistics, while the encoder's output representations are high-level features. These features require transformation from the latent feature space back to the pixel space by the decoder. Thus, the original MAE decoder fits this purpose better. However, the original MAE decoder is not optimal for reconstructing more abstract and more semantic preserving features like the CLIP target. To guide the encoder to learn rich semantic information from the reconstruction target, the encoder's output representations are better to align with the targets without further updates in the decoder. Therefore, the prompting decoder, by freezing the encoder’s output features when reconstructing the masked patches' features, improves the accuracy significantly.

That means, the prompting decoder is specifically designed for the CLIP target and applying it to the pixel target is not beneficial (#3 vs. #1 in Table 5). But when it is applied to CLIP target, it improves the accuracy significantly (#8 vs. #6 in Table 5).

MILAN do not require long training times. When everything else being equal, we prefer the training methodology that converges faster and takes less time to reach the maximum performance. Our method converges to a notably higher accuracy with only 400 epochs of pretraining, while MAE can only saturate to their accuracy with 1600 epochs of training.

content.title: Response.1
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, thank you for your time and comments. We must have communicated in our previous Neurips submission. We have taken your previous comments and suggestions into consideration, by systematically comparing with MVP/MaskFeat, explaining the effectiveness of prompting decoder in our ablation, updating the ViT-Large results to show the model size scalability of MILAN, extending ablation studies to other tasks such as semantic segmentation, and more visual analysis to show that changing the reconstruction target alone (like MVP) cannot achieve optimal performance but the majority of the accuracy gains come from our training methodology and model architecture innovations. Thus, we believe our ICLR submission already addressed your previous concerns. Unfortunately, your reviews were simply copied from previous, disregarding all our improvements made to the manuscript. Nonetheless, we provided our responses to your questions in details as follows:

Q1. The framework follows MaskFeat and MVP, combined with the MAE architecture. The technical contribution is incremental.

A1. MILAN is significantly different from MaskFeat and MVP:

- Reconstruction target. Both MaskFeat and MVP use the same encoder + prediction head architecture as BEiT and only replace the reconstruction target by HOG and CLIP, respectively. In contrast, we enhance the MAE architecture by changing the reconstruction target to latent representations from CLIP image encoder. This is where most of the similarities between MILAN and two previous works lie in. However, since the baseline architectures are different (MAE vs. BEiT), their contributions to final accuracy are different. In MILAN, this change of reconstruction target improves 0.9\% ImageNet top-1 classification accuracy and 1.1 mIoU for segmentation on ADE20K. However, changing the reconstruction target alone is far from sufficient. The following two enhancements further improves the accuracy.
- Decoder architecture. MaskFeat and MVP did not change the decoder of the baseline architecture. But we find that the decoder design is tightly coupled with the reconstruction target. The vanilla decoder in MAE is not optimal for reconstructing latent representations containing affluent semantic signals. We propose a more effective prompting decoder to adapt to our reconstruction target, which further improves 1.5\% ImageNet top-1 accuracy and 2.7 mIoU for segmentation on ADE20K on top of the CLIP target. Our innovation on the decoder design is specific to MAE. This further gain may be difficult to obtain for methods like MVP that use a fully-connected decoder.
- Masking strategy. Both MaskFeat and MVP adopt the uniform sampling strategy same as BEiT, which is indifferent to the semantic importance of different image regions. In contrast, we propose a semantic aware sampling to discriminate more semantically important patches from the unimportant ones. Semantic aware sampling facilitates the model to learn better on more important foreground regions, improving 0.3\% ImageNet top-1 accuracy and 0.8 mIoU for segmentation on ADE20K on top of target and decoder innovations.
In summary, we analyze three highly correlated aspects (reconstruction target, decoder design, and masking strategy), present three innovative components specific to MAE, and have achieved the best accuracy on ViT. We already provided systematic comparison with MaskFeat and MVP in our paper (Table 1 results on ImageNet): MILAN outperforms MaskFeat/MVP by 1.4\%/1.0\% on ViT-Base, and 2.1\%/1.5\% on ViT-Large. We believe MILAN contains sufficient novelty in both training methodology and model architecture.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose masked image pretraining on pretrained CLIP representation. The model is similar to masked autoencoder but predicts image features instead of raw pixels or low level features.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
- Leveraging language to improve representation learning is an interesting and important problem and MILAN is a masked autoencode model that combines pretrained CLIP with MAE. The objective is to predict masked features instead of raw pixels or patches. 
- It shows good results on ImageNet classification, MILAN significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art such as MAE and BEIT. 

Weakness:
- The method is based on pretrained CLIP encoder which is a big limitation since pretraining CLIP is already costly and plugging CLIP into MILAN for another round of expensive pretraining on ImageNet-1K leads to around 1-2 percentage improvement as shown in the finetuning results. 
- This improvement could come from MILAN being pretrained on ImageNet-1K which is in-domain for downstream ImageNet classification.  Without a fair comparison, it’s unclear whether MILAN is better than CLIP or not. To eliminate the domain gap factor, I would suggest the authors pretrain MILAN on the YFCC15M subset and compare it with CLIP. YFCC15M is suggested because it’s smaller than the full 300M dataset therefore more doable, and the CLIP paper shows that pretraining on the YFCC15M subset leads to similar results as the full dataset.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality
- Interesting idea that combines MAE and CLIP for feature space denoising training
- It’s unclear whether the method is better than CLIP which is a module of this method

Clarity
- Mostly clear with some details missing that could be helpful for reproducibility
- MILAN uses a pretrained CLIP VIT encoder, which is pretrained with resolution 224, do you apply up sampling to make it compatible with MILAN at resolution 384? 
- Compared with BEiT and MAE, the advantage is smaller when using a larger model, can the authors run one more size such as VIT-small to show the trend of model scalability?
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors propose a method to do masked autoencoder using CLIP representations by predicting encoded features. The method outperforms MAE and other masked autoencoding methods. However, one critical issue is that it seems improvement might just come from CLIP representations and pretraining on in-domain datasets.

Strength
- The paper is easy to follow.
- The pipeline of MILAN is straightforward and inexpensive to re-implement.

- The idea is similar to knowledge distillation, in this paper, they adopt CLIP. Is it possible to the reconstruct the features from several assistant models? And if the image-language is not strong enough, how much it would affect MILAN? Could you give some discussions?

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new reconstruction target for masked image pretraining method. Instead of predicting raw pixels or low level features, the proposed pretraining objective is to reconstruct the image features with substantial semantic signals that are obtained using caption supervision. The authors propose a more efficient prompting decoder architecture and a semantic aware mask sampling mechanism, which further advance the transfer performance of the pretrained model. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method delivers higher accuracy than the previous works.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

-  Reconstruction targets of existing methods are limited to raw images pixels (both high level visual signals and low-level pixel data), while this paper proposes to use language-image pretrained encoder's output features as the reconstruction target.  The language-image pretrained encoder (CLIP used in this work) can provide more informative semantic signals as a result of using caption supervision. Better reconstruction target helps the model learn better token representations, and further improves the downstream tasks.

- Propose a prompting decoder which only takes the embedding of masked tokens as query, which is more efficient. Besides, The features of unmasked patches into the prompting decoder are frozen, therefore the training of encoder are decoder are decoupled. Encoder can have better transfer performance.

- Due to the CLIP encoder, the proposed method can sample masked patches with the guidance of CLIP's attention scores, and this method can discriminate semantically important image patches from the insignificant background patches, which is better than randomly sampling.

- The proposed method achieves impressive performance on classification on ImageNet-1K, Object detection and instance segmentation on COCO, and semantic segmentation on ADE20K. Also, extensive ablation study shows the effectiveness of different components.

Weaknesses:

- Limitation in generalization and required hardware resources. As the authors have discussed in the limitation section, this paper requires CLIP's output as the supervision signals, therefore its generalization is very limited. While previous methods like MAE does not assume image domain, it can be applied to any domain, such as various domains of medical images. One the other hand, the efficiency might also be an obstacle. If the CLIP encoder runs only once on ImageNet images, then the encoder output as well as the attention map must be stored in hard disk, this data is huge in size. Could you authors add more details about the data size? If not storing this data, then CLIP encoders need to be called in every pretraining steps, which may be slow. Did the authors include the CLIP running time when report pretraining time of MILAN?
 
- Unclear role of the decoder. As the authors claim, the decoder takes frozen features of unmasked patches as the input. The encoder is pretrained under the supervision of reconstruction loss of unmasked patches. Then how does the decoder helps to train the encoder parameters? As the decoder is removed in the fine tuning, what is the role of including a decoder in this method? It seems to me that the proposed method should work without the decoder. While I notice the authors conduct the ablation study with/without the decoder, experimental results in Table 9 shows the decoder helps to improve the representation quality. I do not understand where this help comes from. Actually, the ablation experiment in Table 9 is weak and can not support the conclusion since the `semantic aware knowledge distillation` experiment follows the settings of MILAN. The authors should finetune the settings for  `semantic aware knowledge distillation` and report the results with optimal settings.

- Guided masking method has been investigated in previous paper, such as [1]. The authors include and discuss related methods.

[1] Kakogeorgiou, Ioannis, et al. "What to Hide from Your Students: Attention-Guided Masked Image Modeling." ECCV 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is in good quality overall, and the clarify is good. The novelty is okay but not that good, since it is an improvement of previous methods while having undesired limitations. Reproducibility is weak since no source code is provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents a new masked image pretraining framework and achieves significant improvement compared with previous methods. Extensive experiments are included to show the effectiveness. However, there are some critical limitations and unresolved concerns. I will increase my rate if the authors can resolve my concerns.

content.title: MILAN: Masked Image Pretraining on Language Assisted Representation
content.abstract: Self-attention based transformer models have been dominating many computer vision tasks in the past few years. Their superb model qualities heavily depend on the excessively large labeled image datasets. In order to reduce the reliance on large labeled datasets, reconstruction based masked autoencoders are gaining popularity, which learn high quality transferable representations from unlabeled images. For the same purpose, recent weakly supervised image pretraining methods explore language supervision from text captions accompanying the images. In this work, we propose masked image pretraining on language assisted representation, dubbed as MILAN. Instead of predicting raw pixels or low level features, our pretraining objective is to reconstruct the image features with substantial semantic signals that are obtained using caption supervision. Moreover, to accommodate our reconstruction target, we propose a more efficient prompting decoder architecture and a semantic aware mask sampling mechanism, which further advance the transfer performance of the pretrained model. Experimental results demonstrate that MILAN delivers higher accuracy than the previous works. When the masked autoencoder is pretrained and finetuned on ImageNet-1K dataset with an input resolution of 224×224, MILAN achieves a top-1 accuracy of 85.4% on ViT-Base, surpassing previous state-of-the-arts by 1%. In the downstream semantic segmentation task, MILAN achieves 52.7 mIoU using ViT-Base backbone on ADE20K dataset, outperforming previous masked pretraining results by 4 points.
